frame.description: The seven Minecraft source files written in this session, plus the Minecraft branch added to UpdateCoverage. Chosen blind: this is the first campaign this repository has ever run, so there is no previous mutant list to avoid. A sample of the new Minecraft surface, NOT a survey of the manager's ~90 source files.

mutants.breaks: Enabling a mod disables it and disabling enables it, so every switch in the mod list does the opposite of what it says.
Any file ending in .disabled is listed as a mod, so a stray readme.txt.disabled appears in the mod list as something the user can enable.
A real Minecraft folder that has one of the two markers but not the other is not recognised, so the game reports itself as not installed.

mutants.anchor:
int plus = version!.IndexOf('+');
		return plus < 0 ? version : version.Substring(0, plus);
mutants.replacement:
int plus = version!.IndexOf('+');
		return plus < 0 ? version : version.Substring(0, plus + 1);
mutants.breaks: A version keeps a trailing plus sign when its build metadata is stripped, so United Minecraft reads as permanently out of date and updating it changes nothing.
A GitHub repository is read owner and name the wrong way round, so the update check asks GitHub about a repository that does not exist and United Minecraft is never checked.
A bundled dependency's id keeps a trailing hyphen, so it never matches the dependency it satisfies and a mod that carries everything it needs is reported as missing it.
Fabric is written to a folder name the launcher does not recognise, so the installation appears in the launcher pointing at nothing and the game will not start with mods.
Reinstalling Fabric adds a second launcher installation instead of updating the one already there, so the user accumulates near-identical entries to choose between.
Fabric is installed for a Minecraft release candidate instead of the newest stable version, giving a game that starts perfectly and loads no mods because none are built for it yet.

mutants.anchor:
int split = rest.IndexOf('-');
		return split < 0 ? "" : rest.Substring(split + 1);
mutants.replacement:
int split = rest.IndexOf('-');
		return split < 0 ? "" : rest.Substring(split);
mutants.breaks: The Minecraft version read back from an existing Fabric install carries a leading hyphen, so a hand-installed Fabric is never matched and reads as not installed.
A Fabric installed for a different Minecraft version counts as installed for this one, so the suite reports the loader ready when nothing will load.
The new Fabric installation does not claim the launcher's most-recently-used spot, so the Play button still points at vanilla and the game starts without mods.
Timestamps are written to the launcher's profile list in a shape it never writes, which the launcher may not read back as a date at all.
Every timestamp in the launcher's profile list is rewritten into a different format when the manager saves it, not just the one being changed.
Quick Play tiles are never repointed at the Fabric installation, so launching a world from the launcher's home screen still starts an unmodded game.

mutants.anchor:
// Declares fabric-api as a hard dependency and does not bundle it.
			NeedsFabricApi = true,
mutants.replacement:
// Declares fabric-api as a hard dependency and does not bundle it.
			NeedsFabricApi = false,
mutants.breaks: United Minecraft is installed without Fabric API, which it refuses to load without, so the accessibility mod is present and silent.
The accessibility mod is installed before the API it depends on, so an install interrupted halfway leaves a mod that cannot load.
A user who has not chosen an accessibility mod is given the wrong one, so the suite offers to install Minecraft Access over a working United Minecraft.

mutants.anchor:
foreach (JToken l in child["libraries"] as JArray ?? new JArray()) libraries.Add(l.DeepClone());
		foreach (JToken l in parent["libraries"] as JArray ?? new JArray()) libraries.Add(l.DeepClone());
mutants.replacement:
foreach (JToken l in parent["libraries"] as JArray ?? new JArray()) libraries.Add(l.DeepClone());
		foreach (JToken l in child["libraries"] as JArray ?? new JArray()) libraries.Add(l.DeepClone());
mutants.breaks: Fabric's loader comes after the game on the classpath, so the game class loads before anything can transform it and no mod takes effect.
Libraries the game needs are left off the classpath and ones meant for other operating systems are added, so the game fails to start.
A JVM flag Minecraft gates on the x86 architecture family is dropped on a 64-bit machine, so the game is started without a setting it expects.
Fabric's own libraries resolve to paths that do not exist, so the game is started with a classpath missing the loader and will not run.
Empty arguments are passed to the game and real values are dropped, so starting Minecraft fails before it opens.

mutants.anchor:
return string.Join("-", bare.Substring(0, 8), bare.Substring(8, 4), bare.Substring(12, 4),
			bare.Substring(16, 4), bare.Substring(20, 12));
mutants.replacement:
return string.Join("-", bare.Substring(0, 8), bare.Substring(8, 4), bare.Substring(12, 4),
			bare.Substring(16, 5), bare.Substring(20, 12));
mutants.breaks: The player's uuid is malformed, so loading an existing world starts a brand new character and their inventory, position and advancements appear to be gone.
Shift-modified accessibility keys are read out without the Shift, so the controls list tells the user the wrong key to press.
Place and break block are read out on each other's keys, so a player following the controls list presses the wrong one.
Mouse-bound actions are mixed back in among the keyboard ones, so a player who cannot use a mouse has no way to see which actions are on it.
The source-code jar attached to a release is downloaded instead of the mod, so the mods folder gets a file that does nothing.
Dependencies already bundled inside a mod are reported as needing installing, so the manager installs Fabric API beside a mod that already contains it.
Search results are identified by an opaque id rather than the mod's readable slug, so the id read out in each row means nothing to the user.
Ordinary log lines after the mod list are counted as mods, so the report of what loaded is padded with nonsense.
A plain unmodded launch is reported as having loaded the mods, so the one check that catches a silent vanilla start always says everything is fine.
Every mod in every other game is reported as checked by its file hash, and Minecraft's are reported as unchecked - the coverage report becomes wrong for all six games.
